author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Tablets Make Communication Easier Behind Bars – But Deaf People Are Left Behind
content:
This story was co-published with

 

Truthout

.




Tablet computers have revolutionized communication inside prisons for hearing prisoners. Prison systems from across the country — including in 

New York

, 

California

, and 

Illinois

 — have 

distributed tens of thousands

 of tablets to incarcerated people, which they can use to call home, watch movies, message loved ones, or attend virtual classes (although they are often 

charged predatory fees

 for accessing these benefits). As of 2022, 

25 state prison systems

 had tablet distribution programs, according to the Electronic Privacy Information Center. 




But as the rollout of such tablets continues, many deaf incarcerated people have been left behind. 




Disability justice organization HEARD points out that 

it’s 

unknown

 how many deaf people are incarcerated in U.S. prisons, but a 

2015 report

 by the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimated that 6.2 percent of incarcerated people in 

state

 and 

federal

 prisons have a hearing disability, which would equal about 71,000 people.

author: Maya Schenwar
title: We Must Move Beyond the Era of State-Sponsored, State-Celebrated Murder
content:
This story was co-published with

 

Truthout

.





  Christa Pike woke up on October 6 in a Tennessee hospital with a blood clot and pneumonia, handcuffed and shackled to her bed, having become the first known person to survive an execution via lethal injection. On September 30, the state of Tennessee tried to murder Pike. Instead, it put her through an hour and a half of difficulty breathing as she intermittently gasped for air and was eventually sent into critical condition, in a notoriously “botched execution” — in other words, 

torture

. As Sandra Babcock, one of Pike’s attorneys, 

put it

 on 

Democracy Now

: “Christa Pike … has just experienced the most agonizing attempt at lethal injection in the country’s history.” 






  Conversations in the wake of this torture have, understandably, focused on the exceptional circumstances of the attempted killing. However, this is also an important moment to recognize the depths of brutality in which this country wallows, such that the killing of a person by their own government only tends to make front page news when it is “botched.” It is also a key time to push ourselves to imagine beyond that violence, and to ask: What kind of world can we build, in which an execution is unthinkable?

title: Activists Are Pushing Cities and Companies to Cancel Parking Contracts With ICE
content:

.




The Trump administration’s abduction and deportation machine is multifaceted. There are clear-cut components — agents, shackles, and jails — and less obvious, although no less essential, ones — cars and parking spaces.




In an effort to impede the attacks on immigrants, mayors of some of the country’s largest cities, including 

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani

, 

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson

, and 

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu

, have issued executive orders 

banning Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)

 from using city-owned parking lots and properties.




But even in cities where mayors have banned ICE from using government-owned properties, ICE still has free reign to contract with private companies. After the federal agency 

posted a notice

 seeking “Surge Parking” in 14 cities, including Boston, Wu 

released a public letter

 to 

local parking garage and lot owners

, warning them that if ICE were “to procure such resources, it would constitute an unprovoked and unwarranted escalation, creating potentially significant risks to public safety and halting economic activity across our entire region.”

author: Renée Feltz
title: Tennessee Attempted to Execute a Sexual Assault Victim
content:
This story was co-published with

 

Truthout

.




On September 30, the Supreme Court upheld the execution of Christa Pike by Tennessee after a federal court issued a stay. Shortly after the state administered two doses of lethal injection chemicals, she survived and was hospitalized.




Note: This article contains graphic descriptions of sexual abuse and violence.




Christa Pike was sexually abused and raped from the time when she was a toddler until almost a year to the day before she was arrested in 1995 at age 18 for murdering fellow teenager Colleen Slemmer when the two attended a job training program for troubled youth in Knoxville.




Tennessee officials do not dispute these facts. “I think everybody in this courtroom wishes that those things had never happened to Ms. Pike,” Tennessee Attorney General’s Office lawyer Will Ayers 

acknowledged

 in his 

closing argument

 to a grueling three-day 

hearing

 last month about challenges to Pike’s execution scheduled for September 30. “I think we all wish that we were not here today and that she was not on death row.”




In a new approach, the state’s Supreme Court appointed Shelby County Senior Judge Mark Ward as a “special master” to hear the arguments by Pike’s defense team, including that lethal injection would be cruel and unusual because it could trigger traumatic memories, among other reasons.
